scenes.explain: Released versions never change. A new version plus an eval comparison makes the change traceable and measurable.

items.text: Versions + fingerprints: every result is traceable
A lock file and a test protect released prompts
Evals: labelled cases, a code grader, one score per version
Offline numbers test the pipeline, not the prompt

captions.text: You change one sentence in a prompt, try it on two examples, and it looks better.
Is it?
Maybe it fixed those two and broke five others.
This lesson turns prompt changes into engineering: every prompt has a version you
can trace, and every change is measured on an evaluation set.
You'll version your prompts, and never edit a released version.
Trace every result back to the exact prompt text.
Build a small, labelled evaluation set.
And grade with code, so you can compare versions with numbers.
A prompt change is a code change, and it needs the same discipline.
First, tracing: when a report looks wrong, which exact prompt produced it?
Second, comparing: is the new version better than the old one, on the same cases?
And third, rolling back: if a new version misbehaves in production, return to the
last good one in a single line.
The registry maps each prompt name to its versions.
Old versions stay in the code, so you can always compare against them, or roll back.
Default versions says which one the program uses.
Switching is a one-line change that shows up clearly in code review.
And get prompt returns a version, or a clear error if it doesn't exist.
The prompts command lists every version with its fingerprint: the first eight
characters of a SHA two fifty-six hash of the prompt's text.
Change a single character, and the fingerprint changes.
Every report records these fingerprints, so you always know exactly which text
produced it.
The fingerprints of released versions are stored in a lock file.
This test fails if anyone edits a released prompt in place.
The message says what to do instead: add a version.
And a second test makes sure every new version gets locked too.
So changing a prompt follows a routine.
Copy the current version to a new one, and edit the copy.
Run the evaluation on both versions, with a real model.
Switch the default only if the new version is at least as good, on every case that
matters.
Then lock the new fingerprint, and commit.
An evaluation has three parts.
Cases: real inputs, each with the answer a person decided is correct.
A grader: code that checks each output.
Use exact checks in code wherever you can, and a model as grader only for what code
can't judge, like the quality of advice.
And a score per version.
Same cases, same grader, so two versions finally become comparable.
Start small.
Twenty labelled cases are infinitely more than zero, and you can add a case every
time you find a bug.
Each case pairs a resume with a job posting.
A person labelled every must-have skill: true if the candidate has it, false if not.
Include hard cases on purpose.
Leo's resume says, no experience with Kubernetes.
A careless extractor will see the word Kubernetes and count it as a skill.
Run case runs the real analyzer on the resume and the job, without the advice step,
which this eval doesn't grade.
Then for every labelled skill: was it found in the job at all, and does the verdict,
matched or missing, agree with the label?
Each verdict is simply right or wrong.
The result is a count of correct verdicts, and a list of what went wrong.
Here's the eval for both prompt versions, offline.
Be careful reading this.
Both versions score exactly the same, twenty-one out of twenty-two, because the
offline fake isn't a model: its keyword rules ignore the prompt wording completely.
And look at the one failure: Kubernetes in Leo's case.
The keyword rules saw the word and missed the negation, exactly the mistake that
hard case was written to catch.
With an API key, this same command compares the two prompts on a real model.
That's the number you'd use to decide.
A few habits.
Label cases yourself, and include both hard cases and boring ones.
Turn every bug you find into a new case, so it can never come back unnoticed.
Put every requirement in the prompt itself.
Never describe the grader to the model.
And re-run the evaluation whenever the prompt changes, or the model does.
Quick check.
You want to improve a released prompt.
What do you do?
Add a new version, run the evaluation on both, and switch only if the new one is at
least as good.
Versions and fingerprints make every result traceable.
A lock file and a test protect released prompts.
An evaluation is labelled cases, a code grader, and one score per version.
And offline numbers test the pipeline.
Only a real model tests the prompt.
You now have every piece.
